sections.html:
Building work in the UK runs on contracts, and on a set of statutory rules that sit underneath them. The Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 (the “Construction Act”) gives most parties to construction contracts the right to be paid in stages, to know what they’ll be paid and why, to suspend work for non-payment and to refer disputes to adjudication at any time. Standard forms such as JCT and NEC then set out who does what, when, for how much and what happens when things change.

BuildLaw turns all of that into practical guides: what the rule is, the deadlines that matter, worked examples and what to do next.

• Getting paid: applications, payment notices, pay less notices and your right to suspend.
  • Retentions: how they work, getting them released, and the proposed ban.
  • Contract administration: variations, extensions of time, practical completion and the final account.
  • Adjudication: the 28-day route to a binding decision.
  • Free example notices and letters you can adapt.

• Choosing a contract and procurement route: traditional, design and build, management and more.
  • Which JCT contract? From Minor Works to Design and Build, and the homeowner contracts.
  • Key contract terms: liquidated damages, defects, insurance, termination and design liability.
  • Homeowners and builders: your rights under the Consumer Rights Act and how to avoid disputes.

We start from primary sources: legislation, the Civil Procedure Rules, published contract guidance and court judgments, and link to them at the end of each guide. Pages show the date they were last updated, and changes in the law are covered on our blog. Read our editorial standards.

Our guides are general information, not legal advice. They can’t take account of your contract or your circumstances. For that, use our expert help or speak to a qualified professional.

faqs.a: No. BuildLaw is a free construction law information website. We don’t give legal advice or represent anyone. If you need advice, our services page explains how we can introduce you to independent, qualified professionals, who work under their own terms.

faqs.q: Does BuildLaw cover Scotland and Northern Ireland?
faqs.a: Yes. Our guides are written mainly for England and Wales, and we flag where Scotland or Northern Ireland differ. The Construction Act applies in England, Wales and Scotland, with separate Scheme regulations in Scotland, and Northern Ireland has its own Construction Contracts (Northern Ireland) Order 1997.

faqs.q: Do the payment rules apply to work on my house?
faqs.a: Mostly not. The Construction Act’s payment and adjudication rules don’t apply to contracts with a residential occupier for work on the home they live in, unless the contract itself includes them (some homeowner contracts do). Homeowners are protected by consumer law instead. See homeowners and builders.

faqs.q: Can I use your example notices and letters?
faqs.a: Yes, they’re free to adapt. They’re examples, not templates guaranteed for your situation: always check them against the payment and notice clauses in your own contract, which may set different deadlines or addresses for notices.

Some pages may include affiliate or referral links, and we may be paid when we introduce you to a service provider, at no extra cost to you. This never changes what our guides say. Read how we make money.

blocks.title: Key rules at a glance
blocks.intro: Some of the rules that matter most on UK building projects. Each one links to a full guide with the conditions and exceptions.

items.title: Payment notice: 5 days
items.text: The payer must say what it will pay, and how that sum is worked out, no later than 5 days after each payment due date.

items.title: Pay less before the deadline
items.text: To pay less than the notified sum, the payer must serve a pay less notice in time. Under the Scheme, that’s at least 7 days before the final date for payment.

items.title: Suspend on 7 days’ notice
items.text: If the notified sum isn’t paid by the final date, the payee can suspend work after giving at least 7 days’ notice of intention to suspend.

items.title: Adjudicate at any time
items.text: Either party to a construction contract can refer a dispute to adjudication at any time. The decision is due within 28 days of referral, unless extended.

items.title: Statutory interest
items.text: On business-to-business debts, the Late Payment Act lets you claim interest at 8% above the Bank of England base rate, unless the contract has a substantial remedy.

items.title: No “pay when paid”
items.text: “Pay when paid” clauses are generally ineffective under the Construction Act, except where a party further up the chain is insolvent.

items.title: Courts can order mediation
items.text: Since October 2024 the Civil Procedure Rules expressly allow courts in England and Wales to order parties to engage in ADR, such as mediation.

items.title: 30 years for some defects
items.text: The Building Safety Act 2022 extended the time limit for Defective Premises Act claims about dwellings to 30 years for claims that arose before 28 June 2022, and 15 years for later ones.

items.title: Check the contract
items.text: Find the clauses that apply: payment, notices, variations, extensions of time and dispute resolution. Note every deadline.

items.title: Put it in writing
items.text: Set out the problem, what you want and by when, with your evidence. Many disputes end here. See our example letters.

items.title: Escalate the right way
items.text: Negotiate, mediate or adjudicate, and only then arbitrate or go to court. See your options.
